Published effect-size benchmark sets

Source: R/thresholds-es.R
es_benchmarks.Rd

Look up a published set of effect-size cut-points and return it as an es_thresholds() object with a source citation. Call with no argument to list the available sets.

Usage

es_benchmarks(set)

Arguments

set

Name of the benchmark set. If missing, the available sets are printed and returned invisibly.

Value

An es_thresholds() object, or (when set is missing) an invisible character vector of set names.

Details

setmetriccutssource
"cohen_d"d0.2, 0.5, 0.8Cohen (1988)
"sawilowsky_d"d0.01, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.2, 2.0Sawilowsky (2009)
"cohen_r"r0.1, 0.3, 0.5Cohen (1988)
"funder_ozer_r"r0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40Funder & Ozer (2019)
"gignac_szodorai_r"r0.10, 0.20, 0.30Gignac & Szodorai (2016)
"cohen_eta2"eta20.01, 0.06, 0.14Cohen (1988)
"cohen_f"f0.10, 0.25, 0.40Cohen (1988)
"chen_or"or1.68, 3.47, 6.71Chen, Cohen & Chen (2010)

There is no default set

Benchmarks are field- and outcome-specific. Cohen (1988) presented his values as a fallback for when nothing better is available, and later sets (Funder & Ozer 2019; Gignac & Szodorai 2016) were derived from the distribution of effects in particular literatures. geom_es_zones() therefore requires you to choose a set explicitly.

The cited sources define cut-points; the name of the zone below the first cut ("negligible") is a convention of this package.

"chen_or" is tied to a 1% event rate in the reference group: Chen et al. (2010) show that the odds ratio equivalent to a given d depends on the baseline risk, and is smaller when the baseline risk is higher. Use chen_or_thresholds() for other baseline risks. Under their method the zones are not symmetric on the log scale: the published values are the boundaries above 1, and the boundaries below 1 (1/1.74, 1/4.28, 1/11.40) are computed by applying the method to negative d.

References

Cohen J (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences, 2nd ed. Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum. doi:10.4324/9780203771587

Sawilowsky SS (2009). New effect size rules of thumb. Journal of Modern Applied Statistical Methods 8(2):597-599. doi:10.22237/jmasm/1257035100

Funder DC, Ozer DJ (2019). Evaluating effect size in psychological research: sense and nonsense. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 2(2):156-168. doi:10.1177/2515245919847202

Gignac GE, Szodorai ET (2016). Effect size guidelines for individual differences researchers. Personality and Individual Differences 102:74-78. doi:10.1016/j.paid.2016.06.069

Chen H, Cohen P, Chen S (2010). How big is a big odds ratio? Interpreting the magnitudes of odds ratios in epidemiological studies. Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation 39(4):860-864. doi:10.1080/03610911003650383

See also

es_thresholds(), geom_es_zones()

Examples

es_benchmarks()
#> "cohen_d": d, cuts 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 (Cohen (1988), d)
#> "sawilowsky_d": d, cuts 0.01, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.2, and 2 (Sawilowsky (2009), d)
#> "cohen_r": r, cuts 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5 (Cohen (1988), r)
#> "funder_ozer_r": r, cuts 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, and 0.4 (Funder & Ozer (2019), r)
#> "gignac_szodorai_r": r, cuts 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 (Gignac & Szodorai (2016), r)
#> "cohen_eta2": eta2, cuts 0.01, 0.06, and 0.14 (Cohen (1988), η²)
#> "cohen_f": f, cuts 0.1, 0.25, and 0.4 (Cohen (1988), f)
#> "chen_or": or, cuts 1.68, 3.47, and 6.71 (Chen et al. (2010), OR at 1% baseline
#> risk)
es_benchmarks("cohen_d")
#> <es_thresholds> on the "d" scale
#> negligible: magnitude in [0, 0.2)
#> small: magnitude in [0.2, 0.5)
#> medium: magnitude in [0.5, 0.8)
#> large: magnitude in [0.8, Inf)
#> Source: Cohen J (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences,
#> 2nd ed. Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum. doi:10.4324/9780203771587. Cohen
#> offered these values as conventions for use only when no better basis for
#> judging magnitude is available.
